'''Gail McConnell''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRSE|FInstP|FRMS}} (born 25 August 1976<ref>{{Cite tweet |user=gailmcconnell |author=Gail McConnell |number=770628364558303233 |date=30 Aug 2016 |title=Nothing says 'happy birthday, valued friend & colleague' like a poo cushion & a bottle of gin. They know me well .pic.twitter.com/PnZqUtw7Ay}}</ref><ref>{{Cite tweet |user=gailmcconnell |author=Gail McConnell |number=768935564007596032 |date=25 Aug 2016 |title=Thanks a'body for your birthday wishes and messages. Had a great day!}}</ref>) is a [[Scotland|Scottish]] [[physicist]] who is Professor of Physics and director of the Centre for [[Biophotonics]] at the [[University of Strathclyde]].<ref name="McConnell2004">{{cite journal|last1=McConnell|first1=Gail|title=Confocal laser scanning fluorescence microscopy with a visible continuum source|journal=Optics Express|volume=12|issue=13|year=2004|pages=2844–50|issn=1094-4087|doi=10.1364/OPEX.12.002844|pmid=19483798|bibcode=2004OExpr..12.2844M |doi-access=free}}</ref> She is interested in optical microscopy and novel imaging techniques, and leads the Mesolens microscope facility where her research investigates linear and [[non-linear]] [[optics]].<ref name=epmc>{{EuropePMC|ORCID=0000-0002-7213-0686}}</ref><ref name=scopus>{{Scopus id}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
McConnell credits her high school physics teacher with her inspiration to study science.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://soapboxscience.org/a-different-kind-of-cool-meet-gail-mcconnell/|title=A different kind of cool: Meet Gail McConnell|last=Pettorelli|first=Nathalie|date=2015-06-06|website=SoapboxScience|language=en-US|access-date=2019-03-10|archive-date=9 May 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190509233851/http://soapboxscience.org/a-different-kind-of-cool-meet-gail-mcconnell/|url-status=dead}}</ref> She studied optoelectronics and laser physics at the [[University of Strathclyde]], where she was taught by [[Carol Trager-Cowan]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://index.html/|title=Gail McConnell|publisher=Oxford Biomedical Imaging Network|language=en-GB|access-date=2019-03-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080505195009/http://index.html/|archive-date=2008-05-05|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=carol>{{Cite web|url=https://www.osa.org/en-us/foundation/tributes/women_in_science/prof_gail_mcconnell/|title=Tributes|last=|first=|date=|website=osa.org|publisher=[[Optical Society of America]]|archive-url=|archive-date=|url-status=|access-date=2019-03-10}}</ref> She remained there for her graduate studies, earning a [[PhD]] in laser technology under the supervision of Allister Ferguson in 2002.<ref name=mcphd>{{cite thesis|year=2002|url=https://copac.jisc.ac.uk/id/27104565?style=html|degree=PhD|first=Gail|last=McConnell|title=Nonlinear optical frequency conversion of mode-locked all-solid-state lasers|publisher=University of Strathclyde|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.248368}}|oclc=59348545|website=jisc.ac.uk}} {{free access}}</ref><ref name=":0" />  She was the first member of her family to go to university.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.scientifica.uk.com/neurowire/womeninscience-professor-gail-mcconnell|title=#Womeninscience: Professor Gail McConnell|website=scientifica.uk.com|language=en|access-date=2019-03-10}}</ref>

==Career and research==
McConnell almost worked in [[telecommunication]]s, but was convinced by Ferguson to join Strathclyde's new Centre for Biophotonics.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=http://live.iop-pp01.agh.sleek.net/2017/05/20/a-gateway-to-the-biological-world/|title=» A gateway to the biological world|website=live.iop-pp01.agh.sleek.net|access-date=2019-03-10}}{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> She became interested in biomedical research and increasingly aware of the limitations of commercial imaging.<ref name=":2" /> Here she worked with [[Alison Gurney]] on the development of confocal, multi-photon wide-field microscopes.<ref name=":1" /> Gurney encouraged McConnell to apply for fellowships, and she was a [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]] and [[Research Councils UK]] (RCUK) [[postdoctoral]] [[fellow]].<ref name=":0" /> She developed the world's first white light [[supercontinuum]] laser that could be used for [[confocal microscopy]], as well as laser scanning [[Fluorescence microscope|fluorescence microscopy]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=McConnell|first=Gail|date=2004|title=Confocal laser scanning fluorescence microscopy with a visible continuum source|journal=Optics Express|volume=12|issue=13|pages=2844–50|doi=10.1364/opex.12.002844|pmid=19483798|bibcode=2004OExpr..12.2844M |issn=1094-4087|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Riis|first1=Erling|last2=McConnell|first2=Gail|date=2004|title=Two-photon laser scanning fluorescence microscopy using photonic crystal fiber|journal=Journal of Biomedical Optics|volume=9|issue=5|pages=922–928|doi=10.1117/1.1778734|pmid=15447012|bibcode=2004JBO.....9..922M |issn=1083-3668|url=https://strathprints.strath.ac.uk/45/6/strathprints000045.pdf}}</ref> She attended the [[European Molecular Biology Laboratory]] (EMBL) Practical Course in Advanced Optical Microscopy in [[Plymouth]], which she has continued to support throughout her academic career.<ref name=":1" />

McConnell directs the Centre for Biophotonics and ''Mesolens'' laboratory at the University of Strathclyde,<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=http://www.strathclydemesolab.com/|title=Mesolab {{!}} Optical Mesoscopy at the University of Strathclyde|website=strathclydemesolab.com|language=en|access-date=2019-03-10}}</ref> working on nonlinear and linear optical instrumentation for biomedical imaging.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://elmi2018.eu/programme|title=Programme :: elmi2018|website=elmi2018.eu|access-date=2019-03-10}}</ref> Nonlinear optics allows physicists precise control of excitation parameters, including the chance to tune the duration of laser pules.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ailu.org.uk/adhocpages/gail_mcconnell080827.html|title=Lasers in medicine and biophotonics: Gail McConnell - The Association of Industrial Laser Users|website=ailu.org.uk|access-date=2019-03-10}}{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

In 2009, McConnell began working with [[William Bradshaw Amos]] and built a new lens, ''Mesolens'', that can allow 3D imaging with a depth resolution of a few microns for objects up to 6&nbsp;mm wide and 3&nbsp;mm thick.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=McConnell|first1=Gail|last2=Trägårdh|first2=Johanna|last3=Amor|first3=Rumelo|last4=Dempster|first4=John|last5=Reid|first5=Es|last6=Amos|first6=William Bradshaw|date=2016|editor-last=Bronner|editor-first=Marianne E|title=A novel optical microscope for imaging large embryos and tissue volumes with sub-cellular resolution throughout|journal=eLife|volume=5|article-number=e18659|doi=10.7554/eLife.18659|issn=2050-084X|pmid=27661778 |pmc=5035146 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite web|url=http://www.mesolens.com/|title=Mesolens Ltd {{!}} Mesolens microscope|website=mesolens.com|access-date=2019-03-10}}</ref>  The ''Mesolens'' is a giant optical microscope objective supported by the [[Medical Research Council (United Kingdom)|Medical Research Council]] (MRC).<ref name=":3" /> It can be used to image large biomedical specimens, including embryos, tumours and areas in brain, as well as scanning large areas of samples in a short amount of time.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bps.ac.uk/BPSMemberPortal/media/BPSWebsite/Documents/Publishing/Pharmacology%20Matters/2015/Pharmacology-Matters-December-2015.pdf?ext=.pdf|title=Mesoscope: a novel instrument for imaging microscopic detail in a huge volume of tissue|last=|first=|date=|website=BPS|archive-url=|archive-date=|url-status=|access-date=2019-03-09}}</ref> The lens has 260 [[megapixel]] effective camera and a magic ratio of 8:1, which can even resolve individual bacteria.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":6">{{Cite web|url=https://microbiologysociety.org/publication/past-issues/imaging/article/can-the-mesolens-help-the-microbiologist.html|title=Can the Mesolens help the microbiologist?|last=Society|first=Microbiology|website=microbiologysociety.org|access-date=2019-03-10}}</ref> As the photometric volume can sample such a large area with sub-cellular detail, the ''Mesolens'' may allow for the imaging of rare events.<ref name=":6" /> ''Mesolens'' became a [[University spin-off]], but McConnell decided to stay in academia to explore the physics of biomedical processes.<ref name=":2" /> The ''Mesolens'' generates such large amounts of data that McConnell became interested in [[computational biology]].<ref name=":2" /> The ''Mesolens'' was selected by ''[[Physics World]]'' as one of the top achievements of 2016.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.wired.co.uk/article/gravitational-waves-physics-world-breakthrough|title=Gravitational waves discovery wins Breakthrough of the Year award|last=Woollaston|first=Victoria|date=2016-12-12|website=wired.co.uk|access-date=2019-03-10|issn=1357-0978}}</ref> She discussed the ''Mesolens'' on the podcast ''Not Exactly Rocket Science''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.spreaker.com/user/10814642/gail-mcconnell|title=Gail McConnell|website=spreaker.com|language=en|access-date=2019-03-10}}{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

Alongside the ''Mesolens'', McConnell has explored how laser sources can be used to open [[voltage-gated ion channel]]s, such as [[Calcium-activated potassium channel]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://gtr.ukri.org/projects?ref=EP%2FE025048%2F1|title=The lighter touch: minimally-invasive optical modulation of Ca2+-activated K+ ion channels|last=|first=|date=|website=ukri.org|archive-url=|archive-date=|url-status=|access-date=2019-03-10}}</ref> She has developed a fast-acquisition version of [[two-photon excitation microscopy]] that can be used to image at rates of 100 frames/second.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://gtr.ukri.org/projects?ref=BB%2FM018903%2F1|title=Multi-photon microscopy without scanning for faster than video-rate fluorescence imaging of live cells|last=|first=|date=|website=ukri.org|archive-url=|archive-date=|url-status=|access-date=2019-03-10}}</ref> She created polymer hydrogel beads that are responsive to enzymes.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ulijn|first1=Rein V.|last2=McConnell|first2=Gail|last3=Thornton|first3=Paul D.|date=2005|title=Enzyme responsive polymer hydrogel beads|journal=Chemical Communications|language=en|issue=47|pages=5913–5915|doi=10.1039/B511005J|pmid=16317473|issn=1364-548X}}{{closed access}}</ref> She is working with the Medical Research Scotland to create high brightness [[light-emitting diode]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pureportal.strath.ac.uk/en/projects/applications-of-high-brightness-280nm-light-emitting-diodes-in-bi|title=Applications of high-brightness 280nm light emitting diodes in biomedical optical imaging |publisher= University of Strathclyde|website=pureportal.strath.ac.uk|access-date=2019-03-10}}</ref>

In May 2012, she was appointed Professor and Director of the Centre for Biophotonics at the [[University of Strathclyde]].<ref name=":1" /> She leads the Strathclyde Theme of Physics and Life Sciences and is part of the [[Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council]] (EPSRC) Centre for Doctoral Training in Optical Medical Imaging.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.optima-cdt.ac.uk/supervisors|title=Supervisors OPTIMA|website=optima-cdt.ac.uk|language=en-GB|access-date=2019-03-10}}</ref>

===Awards and honours===
In recognition of her work, McConnell was elected a [[Fellow of the Institute of Physics]] (FInstP) in 2010,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.iop.org/interactions/archive/INTFeb10Digital.pdf|title=Interactions|last=|first=|date=February 2010|website=|publisher=[[Institute of Physics]]|page=3|archive-url=|archive-date=|url-status=|access-date=2019-06-27}}{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh]] (FRSE) in 2019<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.rse.org.uk/fellow/gail-mcconnell/|title=Professor Gail McConnell FRSE|date=2019-03-15|website=The Royal Society of Edinburgh|language=en-GB|access-date=2019-03-15}}</ref> and a Fellow of the [[Royal Microscopical Society]]{{when|date=March 2019}} (FRMS).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.iop.org/interactions/archive/INTFeb10Digital.pdf|title=Interactions: The Newspaper of the Physics Community|last=|first=|date=|website=iop.org|archive-url=|archive-date=|url-status=|access-date=2019-03-10}}{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.rms.org.uk/network-collaborate/science-sections/light-microscopy.html|title=Light Microscopy|website=rms.org.uk|access-date=2019-03-10|archive-date=21 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200921161053/https://www.rms.org.uk/network-collaborate/science-sections/light-microscopy.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.strath.ac.uk/whystrathclyde/news/sevennewroyalsocietyofedinburghfellowsforstrathclyde/|title=Seven new Royal Society of Edinburgh Fellows for Strathclyde {{!}} University of Strathclyde|website=strath.ac.uk|access-date=2019-03-10}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.glasgowcityofscienceandinnovation.com/|title=Seven new RSE fellows for Strathclyde|last=Katasha|website=glasgowcityofscienceandinnovation.com|publisher=Glasgow City of Science and Innovation|access-date=2019-03-10}}</ref>
